title: Netsuke of Boat with the Seven Gods of Good Fortune

image.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Gift of Mrs. Russell Sage, 1910
image.license: Public domain. Released under Creative Commons Zero (CC0) through the Met's Open Access program

altText: A small carved ivory sculpture of a boat carrying a crowd of tiny figures, with a bird among them. The pale ivory is carved in fine detail.

context: A netsuke carved from ivory by an artist named Masahiro in Japan in the late 18th century. It shows a boat carrying the Seven Gods of Good Fortune, a popular group in Japanese folk belief. Netsuke were toggles used to hang pouches from the sash of a kimono.

descriptions.k: Here is a tiny boat carved from ivory. Little people ride inside. They are special gods who bring good luck! A bird is there too. How many small things can you find on this boat?
descriptions.g12: A little boat carries seven gods of good luck. They are carved from ivory, and the whole thing is small enough to hold in your hand. In Japan, this is called a netsuke, and it hung on a belt. Look for the tiny figures and the bird. Who do you think is having the most fun?
descriptions.g35: This netsuke shows the treasure ship of the Seven Gods of Good Fortune, a favorite subject in Japan, where the gods are thought to bring happiness. Netsuke were toggles that held a pouch to a kimono sash, so they had to be small and smooth. The carver, Masahiro, packed many figures into one tiny boat. Look at how they fit together. Why might someone want a lucky boat on their belt?
descriptions.g68: The Seven Gods of Good Fortune, shown aboard a treasure ship, are popular in Japanese folk belief and blend traditions from Japan, China, and India. This late 18th century netsuke by Masahiro puts several figures and a bird into a boat only a few centimeters wide. Because netsuke were handled constantly, the carver shaped forms to avoid sharp edges. How does the carver organize so many figures in a tiny space, and what might the gods mean to the person who wore them?
descriptions.g910: Masahiro's netsuke condenses a lively, crowded subject into an object that had to be worn and handled. The treasure ship carrying the Seven Gods of Good Fortune was a well-known motif associated with luck, especially around the new year. The challenge here is compositional: arranging multiple figures, a boat, and a bird into a compact, snag-free form. Consider how the carver balances detail and mass, and how a sacred or auspicious theme can still carry humor and charm.
descriptions.g1112: Masahiro's netsuke shows how an everyday fastener could carry layered cultural content. The Seven Gods of Good Fortune drew on Shinto, Buddhist, and Chinese traditions and were commonly invoked for luck, particularly at the new year. Compressing a boat and many figures into a single sculpture-in-the-round tests the carver's control of scale and composition. The material, ivory, adds a present-day ethical dimension. How do function, folk belief, and craftsmanship work together, and how does knowing the object's context change what looks charming?

teacherNote.context: An ivory netsuke by Masahiro, late 18th century, showing the treasure ship of the Seven Gods of Good Fortune. Netsuke were toggles for pouches hung from a kimono sash.
directions: Ask students to research one of the Seven Gods and tell what luck that god is said to bring.
Have students design a good-luck charm for a belt and explain how its shape suits being handled.
Discuss historic ivory objects and why present-day laws restrict ivory trade.
